div.head: The Tyranny of Tears: A Comedy in Four Acts
INTRODUCTORY NOTE.
div.p: “The Tyranny of Tears,” a comedy of the emotions, is most ingeniously constructed on the simplest lines; it is a triumph of the commonplace. Played virtually by five characters, and with but one change of scene, it has that specious appearance of ease which is due to dexterity of craftsmanship. It is refreshing, free from theatrical expedients, and save perhaps for the somewhat accelerated wooing in Act Four, knots which we are accustomed to see snipped by the scissors of an erratic fate are here gently untangled by the fingers of probability. The germ of it, a matter of fortunate selection, is a human foible so universal that if a man is not conscious of it in his own proper person, he has not failed to smile over it among his neighbors: that combination of fondness and egoism out of which tyranny is legitimately born. This is the keynote; it announces itself speedily upon the raising of the curtain, and it is never for a moment after obscured by those modern subtilties calculated to provoke discussion among the elect. The hearer equipped with ordinary experience finds himself listening to it with an acquiescent stream of running comment. He knows this alphabet. It spells familiar words, and they come frequently. Here are commonplaces which he has failed perhaps to formulate; but now they flash upon the inward eye with a convincing vividness. This, he sees at once, is a picture of pink and white tyranny, the triumph of the weak. Domestic life has been caught and fixed at the culmination of a strain: one of those dramatic moments when the cord snaps because it has been for a long time fraying. One party to the contract has drawn up a code and imposed it upon his mate. The tyrant has some piquancy; she disarms suspicion because, although a despot, she is masquerading as something else. Another sort of bully we know: the buckram female, loud-voiced, militant, announcing herself, like the mosquito, by a vicious trumpeting. Invulnerability sits on her helm; her armor clanks a little while she strides. But this new tyrant wears another mien. Behold her! a soft-cheeked, gentle-handed ministrant, who would have husbands happy, provided they show the chivalrous courtesy of becoming so in woman’s way. She knows the rules of the game according as her sex interprets them, and it never enters her ingenuous mind that “in marriage there are two ideals to be realized.” Thus does she make her gentle progress, the victim beside her crowned with garlands, but yet a victim. She is the arch destroyer, the juggernaut in muslin.

As soon, therefore, as she is recognized, there is a great pricking-up of ears all over the house. Few are they whose withers are unwrung. Every man among them, primed with his own warfare or that of some defeated chum, settles down to the play, and wives follow suit with a guilty sense that such things are, though “not, thank heaven! under roof of mine.”

A sly humor runs through the piece like a warm-colored thread, a humor always faithful to those universal traits that make us kin. It asserts itself robustly from time to time, once, for a notable instance, in the fact that Parbury is moderately well content in his fool’s paradise until Gunning appears to beckon him out of it. Heretofore he has accepted his experience like a chronic indigestion or a lameness to which he was born; but now comes another man like unto himself, and welds the data of his martyrdom into a cannonball. This man generalizes, and Parbury at once perceives that husbands are not the victims of special visitation, but of an epidemic. The thing is universal. It can be classified; it can even be attacked. He stands shoulder to shoulder with his suffering brothers, and makes his stroke for liberty.

This is everyday life and the dialogue expresses it; the lines are neither too bright nor good for any drawing-room. Here are no sky-rocketings to make the hearer gasp at the playwright’s cleverness, while at the same time they accentuate the difference between his own world and the world as it glitters from the stage. It is the talk to be expected out of the mouths of admirable yet matter-of-fact persons with whom we are quite at home. This is the man you meet at any corner, who is living his life as he conceives it, and is vaguely discomfited when the pattern comes out wrong. He and his fellow puppets are related in the most intimate and delightful way to our own cousins and aunts. It is a group of sharply differentiated types: Parbury, honey-combed with something that passes for amiability; his charming ruler; worldly-wise Gunning, fitted like a glove with amiable cynicisms; the Colonel, clad in rejuvenescence like the spring; and Miss Woodward, an original piquing to the intelligence of any actress ambitious to “create a part.”

The comedy made an instant and striking success, and ran to enormous business until the end of the season. It was revived on January 29, 1902, when the press, previously unstinting in its praise, greeted it with a renewed enthusiasm. The Times says of it, at this second hearing: “No English dramatist of our time has turned out more humorous or more human work than this delightful comedy. Every feeling in it is, as the French say, ‘lived,’ and every word of it tells. There is not a false note, no over-strained sentiment, no over-emphasized phrase in it from one end to the other. Wit it has in abundance, but not in superabundance—wit, that is, that obviously belongs to the speaker and does not delusively suggest the author. Truth, too, it has, but always simple, straightforward, fundamental truth, truth that comes home to men’s business and bosoms, not the far-fetched truth which costs a headache to master it. . . . The Comic Spirit, as expounded by Mr. George Meredith, inhabits it. We laugh at its personages and forgive them with an intimate solace, for in forgiving them we laughingly forgive ourselves. . . . The whole tone of the play is quiet, it soothes, it provokes smiles, chuckles, gentle ripples of laughter. It is a rebuke, a kindly, playful rebuke to the wild and whirling zealots of theatrical violence. We are reminded of the praise which Matthew Arnold bestowed upon the style of Addison—‘perfect,’ he said, ‘in measure, balance and propriety.’”
Equally warm tributes to the comedy as an unusual work of dramatic art were accorded on its presentation, September 11, 1899, at the Empire Theatre, New York, with the following

Of this performance Mr. J. Ranken Towse, in the New York Evening Post, says: “Mr. Drew played Parbury with his accustomed neatness and dexterity. . . . The play, perhaps, may not be quite highly seasoned enough with dramatic incident for the great mass of the public, but its ingenuity, its simplicity, its truthfulness and its humor will commend it strongly to connoisseurs.”

It was afterwards given in the principal cities of the United States with Mr. Drew as the victimized husband, and met everywhere with the same enthusiastic favor. This year, 1902, the play was done into German by Bertha Pozson, and it has been given with extraordinary success throughout the German Empire.

Mr. Chambers’s earlier work lay more in the direction of strong dramas such as “Captain Swift,” “The Idler,” and “John a’ Dreams,” but the comedy of these plays, especially the last, was of a character to foreshadow to some extent the praiseworthy achievement represented by “The Tyranny of Tears.”

Scene.—Mr. Clement Parbury’s study at his house in the neighbourhood of Hampstead Heath. The main entrance leading from the hall is C. A door, R., leads to the dining-room. A glass door, R.C., opens into a garden. The fireplace is C. The room is comfortably and not severely furnished. The furniture is made up of “odds and ends” selected with taste. The couch down L. is a deep and cosy one; the desk or writing-table about R.C. is a large and serviceable one. There is a smaller desk higher up, and near it on wall, R., a telephone apparatus. The apartment altogether represents the workshop of a literary man of careless good taste. There is a touch, too, of femininity in its decorations, and a portrait of Mrs. Parbury is the only picture on the walls, which otherwise are mostly hidden by bookcases.

[For a few moments before and when the curtain rises the noise of street singers is heard. Miss Woodward and Evans are discovered. Miss Woodward is dressed with severe simplicity in a costume of dark colour, with linen collar and cuffs; her dark hair is drawn back from her forehead. Her costume, being well cut, does not conceal the graceful outline of her figure. She is a handsome, innocent, yet determined-looking girl of twenty. She is at the window looking out.

[Raising his voice above the outside singers.] They wouldn’t listen to me, Miss Woodward! [Suddenly the music stops. A pause.] Ah, they’ve listened to Mr. Parbury! [Miss Woodward goes to desk, R., sits.] Mr. Parbury’s a very masterful man—outside his house—isn’t he, Miss? [Miss Woodward favours Evans with a cold stare, then resumes work at desk.] [Aside.] What an iceberg that young woman is! [Telephone bell rings.]
[Miss Woodward goes to telephone and takes line.

[Speaking into telephone—very sweetly.] Yes, are you there?—yes—who are you? Speak a little louder, please. Oh!—Well? Yes—I don’t know—Mr. Parbury’s just coming in now—he’ll speak to you—keep the line.

p.hi: from garden. His hair is untidy; he is flustered and cross. He is an agreeable-looking man of about forty.

div.p: Thank heaven, they’re gone! This house is a mistake! With the nerve force one expends in swearing at street singers one might do some good work. Make a note, please—look for house in secluded part of country. [Miss Woodward makes note.] And make a note—write Times re Street Music; suggest Local Option.
The Saturday Sentinel is waiting to speak to you on the telephone.

Oh, worrying about the article, I suppose. [Goes to telephone.] Hullo! hullo! [Gives them a ring up.] Are you there? [Crossly.] Are you there? Well? [Pause; he listens.] Oh, of course, still harping on my article. I suppose that’s you, Jackson? Oh, well, if you’ll keep this confounded telephone quiet, and send a man to clear the neighbourhood of street singers, you’ll have a chance of receiving the copy in half-an-hour. What? All right, old man. Yes, yes. I’ll send it by special messenger. Yes. Goodbye! [Rings off, and hangs up tube.] That is another mistake—that telephone.
I was afraid you would find it so.

You were right! You are always right! But my wife thought it would save me a lot of correspondence and a lot of going out. [Aside, with a sigh.] I always liked going out. [Aloud.] Make a note, please—get rid of the telephone. [Miss Woodward makes note.] [Goes to top of table, R.C.] Now we’ll get on, please. I’ve promised the article in half-an-hour. [Looks at his watch.] They go to press this afternoon.
[Sits at desk, note-book before her.] Shall I read the last sentence?
[Reading.] “The pity of it is that Mr. Theodore Bellevue seems to enjoy a positively huge contentment of his own achievement——”

[Thinking.] The pity of it—yes—yes, of his own achievement. Yes. [Walks the stage.] Achievement [Under his breath.] Damn the street singers! Damn the telephone! [Aloud.] What is it? Oh—ah! Contentment of his own achievement—er—er— [Dictates.] “One gathers from the complacency of his manner—[Pause]—that his iconoclasm is its own reward—” Er—“What follows in the approval of the unthinking—the applause of the uncultured—” [Pause.] What’s that?
“Makes up—makes up—” Er— [Pulls his hair.] Er——
Enter Mrs. Parbury, L. She is a pretty, fragile, little woman of about twenty-eight, and is charmingly dressed.
I’m not interrupting, am I, darling?
I’ll be ever so quiet. [Comes to couch, sits L.]
Yes, I know, dear—but, I fear—I fear you’ll be rather bored. I’m dictating an article that must be finished this afternoon——

Oh, I shall like it! Go on as if I were not in the room. But oh, how tumbled your hair is. [Rises, goes to him.] I must put it straight. Then you’ll be able to think better. There! Now I can see his clever forehead again! [Goes to couch and sits.]

[Parbury walks up C. and back, trying to collect his thoughts; then he looks at Mrs. Parbury with the wish in his face that she were not there; finally he goes over to Miss Woodward and speaks in a lowered voice.
[At top of table, R.] What was that last?
[Reading in a lowered voice.] “What follows in the approval of the unthinking, the applause of the uncultured makes up.”
Yes, yes. Makes up! [Fidgeting.] Makes up— [Vaguely.] What does it make up? I’m damned if I know what it does make up now? I’ve forgotten.
[Looking up at him with discreet sympathy after a glance at Mrs. Parbury.] Shall I go back a little?
Please do. Cut the other; it doesn’t make up anything.
[Reading.] “One gathers from the complacency of his manner that his iconoclasm is its own reward.”
[Miss Woodward rises, gives him an open magazine, and resumes her seat.
[After glancing at the magazine, and still in a low voice.] “His smug self-sufficiency——” [Pause.]
[Pause. Parbury’s and Miss Woodward’s eyes meet.
Can’t you, dear? I suppose I must unconsciously have lowered my voice.
I’ve an idea. [Comes behind her and touches her shoulders caressingly.] Suppose I finish the article quickly and give it to you to read before sending it away?
[Parbury looks at her, expecting her to move, but she doesn’t.
[With great reproach, and looking as if about to cry.] Clement! [She rises, and with trembling hands begins to gather up her fancy work.]
[Relenting.] Don’t go, dear, unless you wish to.
[More tremblingly and tearfully.] I certainly don’t wish to remain where I am unwelcome.
I thought I had a right to be where my husband was—that the privileges of a wife were at least equal to those of a secretary.

[In a low voice.] Hush, dear! [Turns to Miss Woodward, who has been a secret but attentive observer of the scene.] Miss Woodward, would you kindly run what we have done into type? We’ll finish presently.
[Miss Woodward rises, takes her notes, and crosses to door, L. At the screen she pauses a moment, shrugs her shoulders, and exits R.I.E.
[Parbury passes his arm round Mrs. Parbury.
[Freeing herself.] Oh, no; you wished me to go, and I’m going.
It doesn’t matter now. [Grimly.] The article hasn’t a million to one chance of being finished this afternoon.
Why did you send Miss Woodward away?
Because I hate scenes before other people.
[C.] What! Isn’t there to be a scene? How splendid!
[L.C.] I don’t understand the humour you are in.
I’m in a capital humour, dear. You’ve saved me for the moment from a savage attack on the work of a man whom I respect and admire.
You mean simply that I’ve interrupted your work. You will not have reason to complain again.
No, no. There are things one can’t get over. Perhaps you can explain why it is that Miss Woodward’s presence doesn’t disturb you, while mine does?
Easily. Miss Woodward is a mouse.

I mean she is a table—a chair—a desk—a dictionary—a something useful that is always in the right place at the right moment, and yet of whose presence one is pleasantly unconscious. She is a triumph of the negative.
[Her face is not turned to him.

Positive, my love—quite positive; you bristle with emotions. When you are in the room, one knows it. [Mrs. Parbury takes out her handkerchief and begins to cry. Pause. Parbury, who has gone to desk, looks round inquiringly, then comes down gently and sees what she is doing.] [Aside.] Exactly!
[Wiping her eyes.] Of course I quite understand now that you don’t love me.
[Comes to her, concealing his impatience.] But I do! I do!
Oh no, you don’t! When we were first married you didn’t object to my being in the room when you were working.
I admit I didn’t say so then; I was younger, and had more patience and stronger nerves.
[Turning to him with a gleam of anger.] Then you admit you have always objected to my presence in your study?
[Smoothly.] I admit I have always felt that a writing man’s writing hours are sacred hours.
They shouldn’t be sacred from his wife.
[Gently.] They should be sacred to his wife, dear. [Slight pause.] If you were a writing woman you would understand what I mean.
I’m sure I’m very sorry I’m not a genius, but you understood that when you married me, didn’t you?

Yes, darling, I quite understood that! [He appears to say this quite unconsciously. Mrs. Parbury turns to him deeply offended, then suddenly goes up to leave the room. He quickly meets her, C.] [Taking her hands.] I only knew you were the best little woman in the world!
[Struggling to free her hands.] Don’t, please. I’m going!
To send Miss Woodward to you, since you prefer her society to mine.
But I tell you I’m scarcely conscious of the girl’s existence; anyway, it was you who brought her here. You may remember I proposed having a male secretary.
Yes; to make a companion of at my expense. You were always a man’s man! If I had had more experience I would have known that by the host of men friends you had when we married.
You mean—that I— [Struggling to release her hands.] You are most brutal. Let me go!
Not while you are angry, dear.
[Gently forces her into a chair, R.C.
[There is another slight pause. She is certainly angry, but she doesn’t attempt to leave the chair. He looks down at her, and lays a hand lightly on her hair.

[Brushing his hand away.] Please don’t do that. I am not a child! [Parbury takes a chair and sits next to her. Pause.] Perhaps you will tell me why you have used your superior strength to keep me here against my will?
[Taking her hand.] Do you know that I’m very much in love with you?
You in love with me! You don’t know what love is! All you feel at this moment is the sort of insolent pity the strong have for the weak.
You weak, darling! Oh, come! You know better than that! You can’t be unconscious of your power!

I only meant to remind you that after all you do always get your own way. I’m really very glad, for I’m sure your way must always be the best way. Oh, the power and determination of this little hand! [Holding her hand.] Do let me, with the deepest submission, kiss “The Mailed Fist.”
As it pleases you to be rude to me I shall try to bear it patiently.

I don’t mean to be rude. It’s my unfortunate way of putting things. I kissed your hand because of the real tender love my heart holds for you, and for the same reason I put back this dear, rebellious little lock of hair which has escaped from over your ear. And what a perfect ear! It’s as delicate and fragile as a shell, and it’s just the daintiest pink possible.
[Mollified.] I know my ears are all right, though I think you are making fun of me.
I think I’m making love to you.
[Suddenly taking one of his hands in hers.] Oh, if you only loved me in the way I love you!
I love you in a most excellent way.

But it’s different—you don’t understand. I love to breathe the air you breathe, to hear your voice even when it’s dictating a dry article, to listen to your footsteps, to watch the changing expressions on your face. I live by the warmth your life gives me; you don’t grudge me that, do you?
I love this room because it is yours, the surroundings are yours, the atmosphere is yours. When you are out——
[Gently patting her hand.] Which is not often, dear.
When you are out I always stay here, because here I get most of you; even the thin odour of cigarette smoke is dear to me. Smoke now.
[Gives him a cigarette from his case on table, and lights it.] That’s delightful! [Sniffs the smoke.] But only because it’s you! I used to detest tobacco.
You understand a little now, don’t you?
[Rising.] And you are not angry any more?
Bother the article. I knew it hadn’t a million to one chance!
Then we may have tea in here?

[Standing for moment, C., a whimsical look on his face.] Dear little woman! What a pity she cries so much! [Puts chair up, R.; goes to desk and turns over pages of magazine, still continuing his thought.] What a pity! What a pity!

p.hi: glances up from his magazine as she places the leaves on the desk.

div.p: Do you wish to finish the article now?
Impossible! Tea will be taken here in a few minutes.
[With a touch of indignant surprise.] Here? . . . Oh, I beg your pardon!

Not at all! I said here! [Throws down magazine, goes up to fireplace, C.
Miss Woodward permits a slight groan to escape her.] Eh?
[Parbury looks at her suddenly and keenly as though he had never noticed her before. Slight pause. She arranges papers at desk. He is leaning against the mantelpiece.
Do you know, Miss Woodward, I believe you are more disappointed about that article than I am.
It was so strong! I admire strength.
[Smiling.] You are not then quite the machine one gets into the habit of imagining one’s secretary to be?
[Meeting his eye calmly and fearlessly for a moment.] I should like to be what you wish me to be.
[A little disconcerted.] Humph! [Stands with his hands in his pockets looking at her, while she is busy at the desk.]
[The door, L., suddenly opens. Parbury starts almost violently. Mrs. Parbury puts her head into the room.
Darling, I’ve got rid of a would-be intruder for you. I thought you’d like to know.
Thank you, dear; who was it?
A horrid person named Gunning. There’s the creature’s card. [Throws card into room on to chair by door L.] I knew you’d be pleased, darling! Tea in five minutes.

Gunning! Not George surely? [Quickly gets the card.] It is! My dear old friend; I wouldn’t miss seeing him for worlds! [Rushes to window, opens it, and bends out.] Why, there he is, going across the lawn! [Shouts.] George! George!! Hi! Gunning!!!

[Miss Woodward goes up and looks through window, comes down, and with her handkerchief carefully dusts a photograph of Parbury which stands on book-case up L.C., then looks at the portrait of Mrs. Parbury, which is C. on wall over mantel, shrugs her shoulders slightly, returns to desk.
[C., speaking as they enter.] Quite a mistake! I assure you, my dear fellow, my wife gave orders that I was not to be disturbed, thinking I was engaged upon an important piece of work.
[Looking at Miss Woodward.] Won’t you present me to Mrs.——

[Hastily.] To Miss Woodward, my secretary—certainly! Mr. Gunning, Miss Woodward. [They bow. Miss Woodward moves to go.] Don’t go, Miss Woodward. [Crosses to top of table, R.C.
Gunning puts his hat and gloves on chair, L.] You might very kindly get rid of some of this correspondence for me. [Takes a bundle of letters from desk.] “Dear Sir,—I would esteem it a great favour if you would send me your photograph, together with your autograph.” [Throws letter aside, and reads another.] “My dear Sir,—I have read with the deepest interest and the highest pleasure your deservedly successful novel, ‘The Overthrow of Harvey Masterton,’ and feel convinced that if you knew the story of my life——” [Repeats business.] No one can deal with these people like Miss Woodward.
[Taking off his gloves.] What is your method, Miss Woodward?
It is Mr. Parbury’s—perfect civility, consistent with finality.
Excellent! [Sits and addresses Parbury.] I suppose being a popular author entails a lot of correspondence?
[L.C.] For my part, my correspondence is practically nil.
I have noticed it with pain.
Oh, I’d have written to you, but what was the good of it? I’m not literary, and I’m not married.
And so you’ve kept away for five years.
Five years and three months—for I’ve been married all that time, and you neither came to the wedding nor called on me afterwards.
Discreet! Damned unfriendly, I call it, considering the years we had been pals.
Well, the rest of our old set stuck to you, anyway. What has become of them? Take Wybrow, for instance—an awful good chap!
Wybrow, Wybrow—what has become of Wybrow?
Well, he did a few times some years ago, but——
[Quickly.] Not for me, George, I assure you.
No, no, of course not, my dear chap. Exit Bohemian Wybrow. Then there was Carson—one of the best?
So I heard. You meet constantly, of course?
No, we met them at Brighton one winter some years ago, but I don’t think our wives quite—you understand, don’t you?
Yes, yes, I understand. You dropped the Carsons. But Burleigh——
There was a great spirit if you like; he was your best man.
Yes; he gave me this watch.
Which you still wear. Touching constancy! When did you see him last?
Wait a moment. What is all this interrogation for?
Idle curiosity if you like—study of life if you like. Come, out with it, when did you last have dear old Tom Burleigh to dinner?
[Almost defiantly.] The day we returned from our honeymoon.
[Musingly.] About five years and six weeks ago.
Of course, I see a lot of him at the Clubs. That is to say, I used to when I was still a Club man.
Which now I am not! What does a man want with a Club when he has a home of his own?

Excellent sentiment; but neither the sentiment nor the words are your own, Clement. [Their eyes meet and they burst into laughter.] I know, I know; “and what does a man want with men friends when he has a wife of his own,” and “the husband’s old friends are the wife’s worst enemies,” and “what I say about Clubs is, down with them!”
[Suddenly serious.] What the devil are you laughing at, George? You don’t presume——
I—why, of course not, my dear chap. Only now you see how wise I was not to intrude after your marriage, not to wait for my congé as the other poor boys did! I knew something.
You always did, you brute! I believe you were born knowing something. [Leans on back of sofa.] But seriously [lowers his voice], George, I assure you she’s the best little woman in the world!
Why, of course; it would be impious to suggest otherwise.
[His eyes follow her off.] A perfect wife, and a charming secretary! You’re a lucky fellow, Clement!
Is Miss Woodward charming? On my word, I hadn’t noticed it, but I’m in love with my wife, you see.
Of course you would be the last to discover that your secretary was personally pleasing.
You’re a sinister scoundrel, George, and coarse to a fault. Now, tell me what you’ve been doing all these years—shedding your illusions apparently.
I’ve had none to lose since I grew up. I got rid of mine about the time of measles and whooping-cough.
Not at all. One can’t attain the proper philosophical attitude towards life while one nourishes illusions; one can never gain perspective.
Great man! How beautifully you talk! I suppose you have quite a nice thing in perspectives about with you now.
So much for the journey of the soul. What of the body? Where have you been?
Round the world twice since I saw you.
What did you see on the other side?
Just what one sees on this side; there is always a man—and a woman.

I know you were adventuring in Upper India last year, for the papers were full of a rather fine thing you did—saved a lot of miserable lives—an ordinary, manly, commonplace, heroic, English sort of thing.
Oh, don’t mention that; one was carried away by impulse.

And so we keep our impulses even when we lose our illusions; I’m glad of that anyway. [Then he comes behind Gunning’s chair, takes him by the shoulder, and shakes him.] Old fool! I can’t help liking you as much as ever!

[Rises, puts his hands on Parbury’s shoulders.] Well, I’m glad, because I’ve often been weak enough to regret not seeing you. As for your literary successes, I suppose I ought to congratulate you; but I always knew you’d be a great man, because you never bored me.
[Drily.] Thanks so much. Now tell me how you found me.

By means of the illustrated press—interview with Mr. Clement Parbury—copyright. The author of the “Overthrow of Harvey something” at his pretty retreat at Hampstead—copyright. Snapshot of Mr. Parbury at work—copyright. View of the study from the garden—view of the garden from the study—copyright.
Shut up! You make me blush.
Forgive me—it’s only envy. It’s the envious people who call this a vulgar age, I suppose.

p.hi: places occasional table for tea in front of sofa,

div.p: Now you are to see my wife. How do you imagine her? Large, I suppose, with huge hands and feet and a beetling brow?
When you have had tea, you will go away to dress. You will return here to dinner at eight.
One moment. You will probably meet only my wife’s father, Colonel Armitage, and your dinner will be a fairly plain one, but I promise that your palate will not be outraged.
I really think not, old man. I remember the fate of old Burleigh. And I never even gave you a watch.
George, you hurt me. [Slight pause.] Then you refuse?

That you come yachting with me from to-morrow till the end of the week. I’ve hired a charming little twenty-tonner, one after your own heart—that is, if your heart or my memory hasn’t entirely changed.
[Enthusiastic.] Splendid! There’s nothing I should like so much; and I’ve no special work on hand just now.
Good; we’ll drink of the Cuvée 36, brush up our swearing vocabulary, and I’ll teach you to gain perspective!
[His face suddenly falling.] Oh, the deuce!
What’s the matter? What are you afraid of?

p.hi: wearing a bright smile, which fades when she sees

div.p: Mabel, I want to present you to my dear old friend, George Gunning. My wife, George.
[Gunning crosses to Mrs. Parbury. Shakes hands.
How do you do? I’m very pleased.
[She gives him simultaneously a cold smile and a stiff handshake.
I’m very delighted to meet Clement’s wife.
You’ll let me give you some tea?
Thank you. [Aside to Parbury.] She’s charming!
[Parbury digs him in the ribs. Gunning goes to tea-table. Parbury sits at desk.
[Handing Gunning tea-cup.] I’ve given you no sugar.

p.hi: with MS., which she hands to

div.p: Miss Woodward, you will take tea?
[Takes Miss Woodward’s cup to her, and offers her bread and butter, &c.
You’ve often heard me speak of Gunning, Mabel; we were at Cambridge together.
Oh yes, I remember! [To Gunning.] You were very great friends?

[Comes over and takes his tea.] You see, Gunning had been my fag at Harrow, and my ill-treatment of him inspired a dog-like devotion. [To Miss Woodward.] Let me take your cup. [Adds in a lower voice.] I’ve an idea!
[Miss Woodward goes to desk; Parbury follows her to desk.]
[Assists Mrs. Parbury with the tea service.
[To Miss Woodward in a low voice.] I think I can finish the article in three sentences. Take your notes into the other room; I’ll join you in a moment.
[Miss Woodward gathers her notes and exits R.]

[Pouring out a fresh cup of tea for Gunning.] But of course it’s not in the nature of things that college friendships, however strong, can last always. Time estranges, doesn’t it, Mr. Gunning, and fate drives people into different—well, different ways of life, doesn’t it? Some men marry soon. Are you married, Mr. Gunning?
He has too much respect for your sex, dear. Forgive me for three minutes.
Not married! Well, I should have thought——
That I’m old enough to know better. I admit it.
Well, I was going to say that in marriage a man changes so much. He becomes more—more——

Well, I wasn’t going to say quite that; though, as you suggest it, no doubt it is true. I was going to say more responsible. He enters into a broader, a fuller life; he gains in nobility, don’t you think?
[Amused.] Oh, no doubt Clement has improved enormously!
I’m so glad you recognise that. You may smoke, Mr. Gunning, if you care to.
Thank you. I’ll steal one of Clement’s cigarettes if I may?
Of course Clement was always good and strong and clever. It only wanted marriage to—to——
Well, I was going to say to complete him; but it comes to the same thing, doesn’t it?
I found my happiness when I married Clement.
You had been looking for it?
Of course; isn’t that every woman’s duty?
[Less confidently.] Well, yes, I should think so.
And one’s happiness once found is worth fighting for?
You, I suppose, have never met a woman who could make you happy?
I have never met a woman whom I was sure of being able to make happy.
And, anyway, the state of marriage has always appeared to me to be a state of warfare.

I admit the case of you and Clement to be an exceptional one. I’m talking of ordinary cases—the average marriage; there you will find, according to my observation, an endless war—a war of self-interests, a war of opposing emotions, a war of irreconcilable nervous organisations——
Viewed from the hill-tops rather a pitiful sort of war, in which can be won neither the full joys of love nor the complete glories of battle.
I remain single, Mrs. Parbury, quite without happiness—except in the reflection that I am neither an oppressor exercising a daily tyranny, nor a slave rightly struggling to be free.

Of course I don’t in the least agree with you. [The telephone bell rings.] [Rising.] There’s some one on the telephone—forgive me. [Goes to telephone box and puts the communicator to her ear.] Are you there?—yes—who are you?—the article—yes—no, you can’t have it to-day—no, it hasn’t a million to one chance of being finished. [To Gunning, with a smile.] That’s Clement’s slang, not mine. [Again into telephone.] What?
I say it hasn’t a million to one chance of being finished.

But, my dear, the article is finished. [Rushes to telephone.] [Miss Woodward and Gunning are laughing secretly. Mrs. Parbury stands C., rather confused.] [At telephone.] Hullo! Hullo! Are you there? [Rings violently.] Hullo—oh! is that you, Jackson? . . . what’s the matter? [Rather a long pause. He smiles while listening.] No, no, not at all, my dear chap. What was said was, ‘It’s a million to one you’ll have the copy in half-an-hour’—eh?—yes, those were the very words . . . no, quite a mistake, you don’t listen properly. A messenger has just gone off in a cab with it. What? Yes. [Laughs.] All right! Good-bye!
[Seeing Miss Woodward laughing.] I really don’t know what there is to laugh at, Miss Woodward.
I was only smiling at the messenger in the cab.
[Folds MS. and puts it in envelope.
Yes, send some one at once, please, Miss Woodward.
It wasn’t my fault, dear. You know you did use those words.
My fault entirely. [Aside to Gunning.] Have you told her?
Why, of course not. That’s your affair, my dear fellow.
[His hand on Gunning’s shoulder.] Mabel, dear, we’re going yachting for a few days. I think I want a little change.
[Coming towards them, brightly.] Oh, what a good idea! When do we go? [Parbury and Gunning look at each other.] Are you coming, Mr. Gunning?
[Parbury presses Gunning forward. Gunning looks round at Parbury reproachfully. Parbury goes up stage.

[Embarrassed.] Well, it’s my yacht, Mrs. Parbury, but she’s very small—only a little tub of a thing; and— [Looks at his watch.] By Jove! I’ll never be able to dress and get back for dinner if I don’t hurry. [Gets his hat and gloves, L. Goes up quickly.] I need only say au revoir; don’t trouble, Clement, I’ll find my way out—au revoir!
[Mrs. Parbury, who is puzzled, sits on sofa.
[Calling after Gunning.] Dinner at eight, remember.
[Shuts the door.] Capital fellow, George Gunning!
What does he mean by a little tub of a thing? Surely we’re not——
No, dear, certainly not. You’re quite right. I wouldn’t think of letting you run any risks.
No, dear; that is to say, Gunning and I are going.
Only for a few days, of course.
But—but you never go away without me!
I’ve been working very hard, you know, lately. I feel I want a change.
[Tearfully.] It doesn’t occur to you that I might want a change.
Well, have one, dear. Aunt Martha would be delighted to have you at Oaklands.
I don’t want to go to Aunt Martha. How would you like to go to Aunt Martha?
[Suppressing a groan.] What is it you do want?
[Quickly.] You! I want to be with you! It’s very simple—it’s not asking very much. If you don’t like my being with you, why did you marry me?
Now, dear, please don’t cry! [Aside.] If she does, I’m done for! [Aloud.] It’s only common sense that you can’t go knocking about with a couple of men in a tub of a boat.
Of course I quite know now that you don’t love me.
[With real irritation.] Oh, damn it! [Goes up, but turns quickly and comes down to her.] ’Pon my soul, you make me almost hate——
Of course you hate me. Your old friend has done that for me. You are breaking my heart!

[Who has recovered control of his temper and resumed his natural bantering tone.] Not at all, dear. [Sits at his desk and affects to be busy.] I was only going to say that I hated—now, what the deuce was it I hated?—oh, I know—to see a woman cry. I do think a woman is wise who does her crying in private, and yet—I wonder—they know best—millions to one they know best. I must write something about it.
[Rises, goes to top of table, R. She is wiping her eyes, her back to him.] Of course, you’re going all the same?
Gunning—Gunning!—who’s Gunning? Oh—George—yachting, you mean! Not I! I’m staying here.
[Comes towards him gladly, her arms extended.] Clement!
Eh? Oh, forgive me for a few minutes.
[Reproachfully.] I was only going to kiss you.

[Writing.] All right, dear—presently—presently, there’s a dear girl! [Mrs. Parbury has a slow silent exit, looking back at him.] [He doesn’t look up, but goes on writing. When the door closes, he puts down his pen.] Oh, the tyranny of it! The tyranny of it!

Scene.—The same as Act I. Evening after dinner the same day. The room is lighted with lamps, but as it is a still warm evening, the curtains are not drawn over the glass door which leads into the garden and is open.

[Enter Evans,
L. He places cigars and cigarettes on occasional table, and lights a small spirit cigar-lamp. [Exit.] Voices of ladies and a ripple of laughter heard from the drawing-room, and for a moment the sound made by fingers running lightly and irresponsibly over the keys of the piano. Enter Colonel Armitage, followed by Gunning and Parbury.
Armitage goes to mantelpiece. Gunning selects the easiest chair in the room. Parbury goes to occasional table. Armitage is a well-preserved man of sixty-five, very carefully dressed—something of an elderly dandy.
[Takes one from his case and lights it.
Thank you, I’ll take a cigar. I think, however, I’ll—er—smoke it in the garden. Mabel’s limited appreciation of tobacco——
Oh, Mabel won’t mind—she’s quite educated.
Not beyond the cigarette, I fancy.
[He strolls to the glass door, lights his cigar, and steps out. For a few moments he is still seen, then he wanders away.
Isn’t he? I’m quite fond of him. [Pause. They smoke in silence, Parbury standing at mantelpiece.] What are you thinking of?
I’m not thinking. I’m digesting. I had an excellent dinner.
[Outside.] I’ll have it out here, if I may.
Serve Colonel Armitage’s coffee in the garden.
I notice the glass keeps up well.
Yes, we ought to have capital weather.
Capital! [He is very embarrassed.] If it doesn’t rain it’ll be pretty—er—fine.
[Favours him with a slow stare.] What’s the matter, old man?
Oh, it doesn’t matter. But I think the change will do you good. [Slight pause.] By the way, would to-morrow afternoon suit you for a start?
[Standing with his back to the fireplace, looking up at the ceiling.] I’m not going, old man.
[Effecting a yawn.] I never permit myself to be surprised.

Oh yes, I own I’m disappointed. I looked for a good time for a few days. You were the only one of the old lot available, and you were the best of them. I can’t bear the new lot. They wear strange colours, drop their “g’s,” and get on one’s nerves.
Don’t bother. One simply goes alone. [Discreetly.] The calls of business are often irresistible.
Don’t rot. You know what the situation is.
Mine is one of those poor intelligences that never know without information.
I will, though it does matter. [Grimly.] My wife wept.
Quite. George, what the devil is a man to do?
I knew a man who once interfered between a husband and wife who were disagreeing. The husband and wife each got a black eye. The man got two.
Well, if one dare say so, I fancy you are suffering from the tyranny of a fascinating egoism.
I’m suffering from the tyranny of tears.
What I can’t understand is how a man of your strong nature arrived where you are.
I’ll make an effort to tell you. To begin with, I suppose I’m fairly good-natured.

Or say, if you like, of indolent habit, which after all often passes for the same thing. Then of course I was in love—I am still. One drifted. It’s so easy to give way in little things—really not unpleasant when you’re in love. And then there’s one’s work, which fills the mind and makes the little things appear smaller than they are. I say one drifted.
Sometimes, if I know you, you rebelled. What then?

[Promptly.] Tears! And over such absurdly paltry things! Oh, the farcical tragedy of it all! I wished to go shooting for a few days. Tears! I fancied dining and spending the evening with an old chum. Tears! I would go on a walking tour for a week. Tears! Some one would ask me for three days’ hunting. Tears! Tears, you understand, always on hand. Tears—tears—tears ad—— [Pulling himself up.] No.
No, that would be too low a thing to say.
[Goes up R.C. Takes stopper out of the decanter.
Do you know, Clement, I really like you tremendously.
Thanks, old man. Have some more brandy?
No thanks. [Pause.] Don’t stop. I’m interested.

That’s all. I drifted, almost unconsciously, right up to to-day, for all the world like the man in the moral story-book one read as a child on Sundays, who drifted in his boat on the Erie River towards Niagara. To-night I’m conscious—I’m awake—I can feel the water gliding along the boat’s keel. I can see Niagara. I don’t like it. What the devil’s one to do?
Of course, I shall change it all. I must, but it will be beastly work.
When occasion serves. I can’t go back over this yachting business. I’ve said I’m not going.
Oh, if the exigeant women only knew—if they only knew!
Talking of brandies, this is Hennessy ’63. Have some, Colonel?
Miss Woodward and I are boring each other. Shall we come to you, or will you come to us? [Gunning and Armitage rise.] There, the question’s answered.
[To Mrs. Parbury.] You were playing the piano just now?
Yes, but I play wretchedly nowadays. I gave up practising when we married.
One should never give up an accomplishment.
You used to play charmingly, Mabel.

You thought so, dear, and that was enough for me. [She rises and crosses to C.] Why don’t we sit in the garden? It’s a perfect night. [Colonel strolls off to garden.] [Mrs. Parbury goes to Parbury, who is standing by fireplace, and takes his arm. In a low voice.] Are you still angry?
[As they go out to the garden.] I angry with you! Nonsense. [He pats her hand.] Poor little woman! Poor little woman!
[Crossing to R.C. top of the table.] Are you not coming, Miss Woodward?
No, thank you. I have some work to do.
But you seem to me to be always working.
I needn’t, you know. I do it because I like it.
Correcting proof sheets of a new novel. It will save Mr. Parbury the trouble of doing it to-morrow.
I wanted you to talk to me.
What do you wish to know?
Will you go away and leave me to work if I tell you?

[Putting down her pen, and resting her cheek on her hand.] I’m the thirteenth daughter of a parson. Why my parents had thirteen daughters, I don’t know; but I suppose it was because they are very poor. We were all given the names of flowers—Rose, Lily, Tulip, Mignonette—I can’t remember them all—but Hyacinth fell to my lot. Why we were called after flowers, I don’t know; but I suppose it was because we are none of us the least like flowers. My eldest sister married my father’s curate. I don’t know why, but I suppose it was because she came first and is the plainest in the family.

[Speaking in an even, emotionless way.] Two other of my sisters run a Kindergarten, and one other is a governess. Personally I would rather be a domestic servant. The others remain at home, help in the house, and await husbands. I fear they will wait in vain, because there are so many women in our part of the country and so few men. For my part I seized an early opportunity of learning shorthand and typewriting—and—well, here I am. Now you know the story of my life.
I’m afraid it was deuced impertinent of me to ask.
And so you have found your happiness.
Oh no. I’ve only just started to look for it.
Very. Have you ever been poor?
Yes, at one time—had to pawn things.

I mean being one of fifteen in family—large inferior joints to last for days—hot, cold, hashed, minced, shepherd’s pie—[Gunning shudders at this]—too much potatoes—too much boiled rice—too much bread and dripping—too much weak tea—too much polishing up of things not worth polishing up—too much darning on too little material—and for ever giving thanks out of all proportion to the benefits received. I wish some one would write the history of a hat or a frock—I mean a hat or a frock that has marched steadily and sullenly under various guises through an entire family such as ours, from the mother down to the youngest girl. What might be written of the thoughts that had been thought under such a hat, or of the hearts that had felt under such a frock!
Why don’t you write the story?

Perhaps some day I shall try. [Returns to her work.] In the meantime you ought to go. You promised, you know. You have nothing more to learn. I don’t think in all my life I’ve talked so much about myself as I have to you, a stranger.
[She keeps her eyes on her work.
You have been engagingly frank. I do hope I shall have another opportunity——
Not at all likely, Mr. Gunning. [Pause.] Goodnight. [Still without looking up.]
[Gunning looks at her, goes up to the window, turns, looks at her again.
[Miss Woodward goes on with her work for a few moments, then drops her face on her hand in her favourite attitude.

[Soliloquising.] Rather than go back, I—well, I know I’d rather die. [She looks over the pages for a moment or two, then yawns slightly; she gathers her pages together and places a paperweight over them.] That will have to do. [She rises, looks off R.] There was actually a man ready to take a sort of languid interest in me. Quite a new experience. [She takes up Parbury’s photograph and speaks to it.] You don’t take an interest in me of any kind, do you? [To the photograph.] You never will, and I don’t think I want you to. But I do want to stay near you, because you are so strong—
—and so weak, and so kind, and so foolish.

[Mrs. Parbury has come down and is watching her unobserved. Miss Woodward slowly raises the photograph to her lips. The cup and saucer drop from Mrs. Parbury’s hand to the floor and are broken. Miss Woodward, much startled, slowly turns towards Mrs. Parbury, and their eyes meet. There is a pause. Suddenly, with a quick movement, Mrs. Parbury snatches the photograph from Miss Woodward.
How dare you! How dare you! [Long pause. She is almost breathless. Then she partly regains self-control.] What train do you intend taking?
I mean for your home, of course.
[Moves as if she had received a blow, and clasps her hands together.] I am not going home.
Oh, indeed you are. You don’t suppose you can stay here, do you?
How dare you ask that when I have just caught you in the act of kissing my husband’s photograph?
That was in a moment of abstraction. I wasn’t even thinking of Mr. Parbury.
Oh! And you are the daughter of a clergyman! [She goes up and fetches the A.B.C. from bookcase, and offers it to Miss Woodward.] Here is the A.B.C.
[Turning away.] I have no use for it just now, thank you.

Then I’ll look you out an early morning train myself. [Sits L.] Let me see—[turning over leaves]—Carfields, Worcestershire, isn’t it? Here it is. 7.20. I suppose that’s too early. 9.35; that will do. Please understand you are to take the 9.35 from Paddington in the morning.
[Firmly.] I shall do nothing of the kind.
[Ignoring the remark.] In the meanwhile there is no necessity that my husband should know the reason of your going. You can make some excuse. I wouldn’t have him know for worlds.

Of course he shall never know from me—but I want you to quite understand, Mrs. Parbury, that I am not going to Carfields to-morrow. Rather than go home under the circumstances I would starve in the gutter.
Well, you must find a lodging till you get other employment. You will have a month’s salary, of course. Anyway, I’m determined you leave this house in the morning.
[Goes up C. Puts A.B.C. on chair up L.C.
Is there any real occasion for my leaving?
Haven’t you sufficient delicacy of feeling left to teach you that?

[Warmly.] I don’t think I need lessons of delicacy of feeling from you. [Slight pause.] I’m sorry I said that, and it means a great deal for me to say I’m sorry. I’m sorry too about the photograph. I think it all might be forgotten.
After all, I’m only a girl; and I’ve worked very hard for Mr. Parbury. I think you might be more lenient.
[At fireplace.] I’m very sorry for you, Miss Woodward; but I owe a duty to myself and to my husband. You must go in the morning.

I suppose I ought to be a lady and go, because you, the mistress of the house, wish me to. But I don’t feel a bit like a lady just now. I only feel like a poor girl whose chances in life are being ruined for a very small and innocent folly.
Well, what does all this mean?
[Fiercely.] It means that I am in Mr. Parbury’s employment, not yours, and that I will take my dismissal from him only.
Oh, I can promise you that. [She calls into the garden.] Clement!

[Miss Woodward throws a hard look after her. Then her eyes fall on the broken cup and saucer. She stoops, collects the fragments, and puts them in waste-paper basket. Then she goes to desk, sits and works on proof sheets as before.
Working again, Miss Woodward! Really, you are indefatigable!
I’m only correcting these proof sheets.
No doubt Miss Woodward wishes to finish the work to-night, as she is leaving to-morrow.
I think Mrs. Parbury is mistaken.
[To Mrs. Parbury.] What do you mean, dear?
I can’t tell you. It is not a thing you would understand. It is simply impossible for her to remain. In her heart she knows I am right.
[Slight pause. Parbury goes to Miss Woodward.
You have no wish to go away?
Not while you wish me to remain.
Do you know why my wife wishes you to go?
I’m sorry I can’t. I’ve promised. But—[with a look at Mrs. Parbury]—I don’t think that Mrs. Parbury’s reasons are adequate.
[To Mrs. Parbury.] Have you anything more to say?
I have only to repeat that it is quite impossible for Miss Woodward to stay.

Well, I have made up my mind that there is something very foolish under all this, and I shall not allow it to deprive me of Miss Woodward’s services. [Mrs. Parbury looks surprised.] I don’t mind saying in her presence that she is invaluable to me. I should never be able to replace her. [Sense of relief on Miss Woodward’s part.] Now, come. [Looking from one to the other.] What is it? A tiff—a stupid misunderstanding? Oh, you women, why will you fuss about little things? Make it up, do. Think of “The Roll of Ages.” Shake hands, cry, embrace, kiss, or whatever your pet method may be. Weep if you like, though personally I’d rather you didn’t. Anyway, as far as I am concerned, the incident is closed.
[Doggedly.] Miss Woodward leaves this house in the morning.
[Looks at his wife for a moment, then turns to Miss Woodward.] Miss Woodward, would you be so very kind——
[He opens the door for her with great courtesy. Miss Woodward bows, and exits L. He comes to C.
[Turning to him with assumed brightness.] Now, darling, it will be different. Of course, I couldn’t say much before her. You were quite right to be nice and courteous to her now she is going.
But I assure you she is not.

[They are C.
Mrs. Parbury takes his arm caressingly.
But she is—believe me, she is. Of course, we don’t want to be hard on her, and she shall have a month’s salary and a strong recommendation.

[Disengaging his arm.] My dear Mabel, I absolutely refuse to act in the dark. I hate mysteries. If you care to tell me what all this bother is about, I’ll judge for myself what’s the right thing to do.
I can’t—it’s impossible. There are some things that men can’t be trusted to know about. You must leave this matter to me.
That I quite decline to do.
[She again takes his arm and talks rapidly, gradually rather hysterically, towards the end appearing about to cry.

Darling, do listen. You don’t understand. You have never been like this with me before. I’m sure I’m not asking very much. You can easily get another secretary. Another time you shall have a man one, as you originally wanted to. You were right, dear—you often are. [Parbury rises; crosses to R.
Mrs. Parbury follows him.] Darling, do be reasonable. I’ve been a good wife to you, haven’t I? I’ve always respected your wishes, and not bothered you more than I could help. This is only a little thing, and you must let me have my own way. You must trust me absolutely, dear. You know anything I would do would only be for your good, for you know that I love you. [She takes out her handkerchief.] I adore you, darling. You must give way—you must—you must!
[Stepping back from her.] If you cry I shall leave the room.
[With her back to the audience, in a low voice.] I wasn’t going to cry.
[Mrs. Parbury puts her handkerchief away and turns.
I had no intention of crying, dear. [Parbury still writes. Pause. She comes to desk.] Shall I write out an advertisement for you, dear?
No. My mind’s made up. I shall not change my secretary.

[Rises and goes to her.] Listen, my dear Mabel. Perhaps I’m a good deal to blame for the pain you are going to suffer now, and I’m very sorry for you; in many ways you are the best little woman in the world. I’ve been weak and yielding, and I’ve gradually allowed you to acquire a great deal more power than you know how to use wisely.
Really, Clement, you must be raving.

Listen, my dear, listen. What’s been the result? You’ve taken from me my habits. You’ve taken from me my friends. You’ve taken from me my clubs. You’ve taken from me my self-esteem, my joy in life, my high spirits, the cheery devil that God implanted in me; but, damn it, you must leave me my secretary.

[Excitedly walking the stage.] Oh, I understand now. You use this exaggerated language, you make these cruel accusations, you work yourself into a passion, because you have grown to think more of Miss Woodward than of me.
Now you know that to be a purely fantastic interpretation of what I said. [She takes out handkerchief.] I observe with pain, too, that you are about to cry again.

[Puts handkerchief up her sleeve, controls her anger, and becomes very determined.] You are quite wrong. Probably I shall never again know the relief of tears. Your callousness and obstinacy seem to have dried up all the tenderness in me. Miss Woodward leaves this house in the morning, or I leave it to-night.
[Coming to her.] Oh, come, come, Mabel, that is too ridiculous.
I’m very, very serious. Please, for your own sake, understand that. Which is it to be?
There, dear, let’s drop it now. Don’t you think domestic squabbles like this, besides being boring, are just a little—may one say it, vulgar? Let’s go back to the garden.
[Shrugs his shoulders.] Of course, you know I’m decided. Miss Woodward stays.
[She goes to bell L. of fireplace and rings. Parbury goes up, takes a book, and negligently turns over the leaves, secretly, however, watching his wife. Pause until
I needn’t keep you from your friend, Mr. Gunning, any longer.
I’m all right here, dear; I’m perfectly contented. [He turns over leaves.] There is such a wise passage here. I’d like to read it to you. [She makes a gesture of irritation.] No! Well, it must keep.
Caroline, I shall want you to pack a few things for me.
I’ll come upstairs and show you.
[Rising from his leaning attitude against table up stage, putting down the book, and coming down two steps.] You foolish little woman. You know this is impossible. Be reasonable.
[With a gesture conveys that the subject is closed and returns to his former attitude.] I think I have a right to ask what you propose doing.
I propose going home with my father.
[The laugh of the Colonel is heard in the garden. Then he appears at the entrance, still laughing. Gunning appears behind him. The Colonel enters. Gunning remains at the window smoking.
[To Parbury.] That’s really the funniest thing I’ve heard for years. Have you heard that story, Clement?
Story of—[Then he sees Mrs. Parbury.] Oh, quite a drawing-room story, believe me, dear.
Father, I wish to speak to you.
[Crosses to sofa, L. Sits. Parbury exchanges a look with Gunning.
[Coming down quickly.] Mrs. Parbury, I must reluctantly say good-night. Your charming house is almost in the country, and I’ve to get back to London. I thank you for——
[Interrupting.] Please don’t go, Mr. Gunning. It’s quite early, and Clement and you, as such very old friends, must still have a great deal to talk about.
[Taking Gunning’s arm.] No, George, you really mustn’t go.
I assure you, my dear chap——
[Interrupting.] But I make it a personal favour. Dear student of life, stay and observe.
Dear father, I wish you to take me home with you to-night.
Don’t question me. [Puts her hand on his shoulder.] You love me, don’t you?
Naturally, my dear. But nowadays, of course, I take second place.
I thought so too, but I was wrong. Wait for me a few minutes.
[Hesitatingly, after glancing at Parbury and again at his daughter.] One moment, Mabel. This is all so sudden.
Father, do you hesitate to receive me?
Oh! I was thinking, my dear, that unfortunately there is no mother to receive you now. I’m only an old bachelor, and you’ll be—er—give me a word.
[Kisses him, and goes to door, L. She looks across the room at her husband, and then whispers to herself.] He’ll never let me go.
[To Gunning.] She’ll not go, my dear fellow.
Humph! You think not? Anyway, I must,
The domestic atmosphere is volcanic, and I feel remorseful.
Nonsense, it had to come. You must see me through it now.
How beastly selfish you married men are!
She proposes going home with you.
[Smiling confidently.] I don’t think she’ll go.
[To Colonel.] Your carriage, sir. [Parbury looks uneasy.]
[Whistles. Looks at his watch.] I think she means it. I ordered my man to wait in the Avenue till he was called. Mabel has evidently had him called.
I don’t wish to be in the least degree meddlesome; but, well, there it is!
The question, I suppose, is what’s it all about?
Well, yes. I suppose that’s it; although I don’t in the least wish to know.
You hear, George; what’s it all about?

[Down R., almost angrily.] Now, how the deuce should I know? Colonel, you would be very kind if you would use your authority to prevent Clement dragging me into his domestic difficulties. Married men have a cowardly way of endeavouring to involve their friends. Perhaps you have noticed it.
I have, Mr. Gunning. My experience of married life extended over a period of twenty-six years.
May one discreetly express the hope that they were very happy years?

Very happy years, with, however, I must admit, intermittent troubles. Mabel’s mother was one of the best women in the world, but, if I may say so without disloyalty, she was just a little—a little—er—give me a word.
Admirably. Perhaps you have noticed in Mabel the slightest tendency? Eh?
Her mother’s jealousy, too, was something amazing. I hope I’m not conceited, but in those days I was just a little—er—popular, and perhaps I ought not to confess it, a little—er—give me a word.
[With affected severity.] Clement, I hope you are not too human?
Quite the contrary, I assure you, Colonel.
Then why—I suppose, after all, it is my duty to ask—why does Mabel come home with me to-night?
She is simply using pressure to get her own way in a matter in which I think her way the wrong way.
Gad! they do like their own way, don’t they? Well, no doubt she’ll be more reasonable to-morrow. I think I may trust you.

p.hi: She has put on a hat and a cloak.

div.p: [Going to Gunning.] You’ll forgive me, I’m sure, Mr. Gunning. Good-night. You’ll have Clement all to yourself.
[They shake hands. Parbury joins her, C.
[In a low voice.] Don’t go, Mabel. It’s very foolish.
[Softening.] You could prevent me if you wished.
[Hard again.] Which way is it to be?
[Alone, C.] Good heavens! He’ll really let me go. [Hesitates for a moment, then draws herself up.] Come, father.
[Comes down, a little astonished.] By Jove, she’s really going!
[Gunning sits. Parbury stands C., listening. Pause. Then there is the noise of a carriage door being shut.
[Parbury somewhat unsteadily lights a cigarette. He then catches Gunning’s eye. They look at each other.
Scene.—The Rose Garden at Parbury’s house. A garden table, seat, and chairs. The next morning.

[Enter Miss Woodward. She is dressed simply, but less severely than before. Her hair is dressed more loosely. She carries a little basket full of roses. She places some roses upon the table, which is laid for two for breakfast. She plucks more roses and fastens them in her dress. Meanwhile she hums an air and conveys the impression of being happier than in the previous Acts.]

[Enter Gunning,
R. He wears a light morning suit, a round hat and brown boots, and carries a stick and gloves.]
Shall I resist the temptation to pay you a compliment?
I thought you would say so. All the same, I feel it to be a deprivation.
Isn’t that remark itself the cloven foot of compliment?
Eh—well, perhaps it is. I’m sorry.
Unlike me? What does that mean?
That it isn’t much in your way to pay women compliments.
I hope you are doing me an injustice.
I don’t think so. You haven’t a very lofty opinion of women as a sex, have you?
Pretty well—pretty well; but what makes you think so?
I heard you talk, you know, yesterday afternoon.
Oh yes; one does talk a lot of rot sometimes, doesn’t one?
No. But he is sure to be in a few minutes. He is generally early. Breakfast, as you see, will be served here. Perhaps—perhaps you would rather wait indoors.
No; I’ll stay here if I may. . . . I’m afraid we made rather a late night of it.
You had much to talk of. I envy people with pleasant memories.
I don’t remember that we talked much of old times. I think we talked of the present.
[Rather hardly.] Then my envy has flown.
You are right. This affair is rather boring.
Miss Woodward, you are a triumph of the inscrutable.
[Leaning on chair, L.C.] I’m sure that is very clever, because I can’t quite understand it.
Quite seriously, Miss Woodward, you interest me more than any person I have ever met.
Do you always say that to girls, Mr. Gunning?
You ought to. I’m sure it’s very encouraging.
Are you quite sure you wouldn’t rather wait indoors?
Oh, quite. I like being here.
But I’m sure you find it difficult getting down to one’s level. I often think that the very wise must be very lonely.
I’m sorry. [She sighs.] We don’t seem to get on very well, do we?
[With sincerity and coming close to her.] I’d like to get on well with you.
[Pause. They look in each other’s faces, both at table.
Will you give me a rose?

Good-morning. I hope I haven’t kept you waiting. Oh, you are here, Miss Woodward. Good-morning. [Looks at the table.] And you have managed to find us some roses. How very kind of you! [Miss Woodward gives him letters. He runs them over.] No, no, no, no! Will you kindly see what they’re all about? [She is about to go.] Oh, not now—after breakfast will do.

Really! I suppose I’m horribly late. [Looks at his watch. Then, noticing the roses she carries in her hand.] How very beautiful they are! Look, George! [She selects one and hands it to him.] For me? Thank you. [He fastens it in his buttonhole.]
Not at all. But, really, you married men are very tiresome.
Oh, I see—wanted a rose yourself. Shall I call Miss Woodward back and ask for you?
Don’t trouble. I’ve done that myself.
You have? Ha, ha! [Begins to laugh, but stops suddenly.] Oh! [Holding his head.] Dear, dear, what a head I have!
You haven’t asked after my head.
[Sits at table.] Your pardon. How is it?
[Sits at table.] I’d like to sell it this morning. Do you know, Clement, I’m not quite certain about that whisky of yours.
I am. It’s fifteen years old.
But you always had a way of mixing your drinks over-night and growling in the morning.
[Drawing up his chair.] Put it at that, if you like. I do know that I always had a way of disliking you particularly in the morning. I regret I don’t appear to have grown out of it.
I’m so glad. I hate being too popular. [Evans offers bacon to Mr. Parbury. He pushes the dish away.] Take it away. Have some bacon, George?
[Takes a piece of toast, looks at it, then puts it down.
I must say I think your display of temper is in the worst possible taste under the circumstances.
[Buttering toast.] What do you mean by “under the circumstances”?
You know what I mean. How much sleep do you think I’ve had?

I’m sure I don’t know. What concerns me is that you detained me in this outlandish place—what county is it?—till past three o’clock, and then insisted, with alcoholic tears in your eyes, on my returning to breakfast.
[Lifts the lid of the tea-pot, then of the coffee-pot, and closes them gently with a look of distaste.] No, not this morning. Still, we must drink something. What shall it be?
Perhaps we had better split a bottle.
Please be frank. Do you mean Bass or champagne?
Champagne, of course. [He calls loudly.] Evans! Evans!

[Exit Evans,
L., wearing a discreet smile.
It’s a thing I haven’t done for years—taken wine in the morning.
In what I may venture to describe as the pre-domestic period it was rather a way of yours.
Ours, if you prefer it. Where’s the salt?
There it is, right before your eyes. Why don’t you look?
Pass the mustard, please. What a good chap you were in those days.
Thanks, I’ve got some. Always what?
It’s quite pleasant out here, isn’t it?
Delightful. You were saying I was always——
Of course, being about me it wouldn’t matter.
Well, I was going to say you were always rather sour-natured.
[He takes up a daily paper and glances through it, continuing to do so while Parbury speaks.
And that has, I fancy, quite unconsciously to you, I am sure, a disturbing influence on others of happier nature.
Take yesterday, for instance. Of course, you didn’t intend it. I wouldn’t suggest that for a moment. But, damn it, look at the result?
[In the same manner as before.] Yes.

[Taking the top off his boiled egg.] Simply deplorable. I’ve broken loose from my moorings. I’m at the mercy of every breeze. I feel that I’ve lost moral stability. Confound it, why doesn’t that champagne come?

p.hi: with champagne. Pours out two glasses and hands them to

div.p: I’m not quite certain that for a man like me—[Gunning groans and returns to his newspaper]—a man, if I may say so, of generous instincts and large sympathies—a groove isn’t a good thing, even if it be a little narrow. Of course, for a man of your nature, it’s a different matter.
[Suddenly puts down the paper, draws his chair closer to the table, and takes an egg with apparent cheerfulness.] What were you saying, old man?
[Fingering the rose in his buttonhole.] Dear, dear, how cross you are to-day!
Excuse me, sir, may I speak to you?
Well, sir, so to speak, she wants to know where she stands.
[Looks at Evans, then at Gunning.] How can I help her?
I mean, sir, or rather she means, now mistress has gone away——
I presume my wife has a right to go away for a few days without cook’s permission.

Yes, sir, certainly. But excuse me, sir; there’s been gossip. Emma, the ’ousemaid, accidentally overheard something between Mrs. Parbury and her maid. Servants is as nervous as race-horses, sir, and cook’s nerves is particularly sensible. So to speak, dismoralisation’s set up in the kitchen.
Well, you had better go and set it down again, Evans, and don’t bother me any more.
Yes, sir, certainly. Excuse me, sir, I was to ask you who cook is to take her orders from.
In my wife’s absence, from me, of course.
[Staring slightly.] Why, has Miss Woodward given any orders?
[There is a pause. Parbury and Gunning exchange looks.
[Parbury slowly drinks a glass of wine. Gunning also drinks. Parbury re-fills the glasses.
Good-morning, Colonel. [He rises and shakes hands.] Not in the least.
[At back of table, C.] Good-morning, Mr. Gunning.
Thanks, yes, but poorly. I didn’t get to bed till four.
And then I had but little sleep.
[With a touch of asperity.] Your troubles, Clement, you have, of course, brought upon yourself; but I think it’s a little hard on your friends that they should be made to suffer with you.
[Tapping the champagne bottle with his stick.] What’s this! Some new kind of table water, I suppose.
Champagne at this hour! Well, I suppose you know best how to regulate your life. Have you an extra glass?
It’s a thing I haven’t done for many years.
I trust, Colonel, you won’t accuse me of leading you from the path of morning abstinence.
Really, Clement, I think this display of ill-humour is scarcely in—er—give me a word.
Exactly! Good taste, considering that we are suffering from the effects of your domestic—er—er——
I quite agree with you, Colonel.

Look at your friend there. If he’ll allow me to say so, he’s put on ten years since yesterday. Look at me! Last evening, I suggest—I hope I’m not conceited—I suggest I didn’t look a day over forty-seven.
While to-day—what would you say, Mr Gunning?
[Looks at him critically, then falls back in his chair.] Fifty-two.
[Parbury looks savagely at Gunning, throws his apple on table, and turns away.
I feared so; but I like you for your frankness.

p.hi: with tumbler on tray; he places tumbler on table, and collects the breakfast things. Pause.
lights his cigar with a match

div.p: You haven’t asked me if I have a message for you.
[After a glance at Evans.] Yes; Allerton doesn’t run any of his horses. Death in the family, you know.
So I heard. That will do, Evans. You may leave the champagne.
[Watches Evans off; then to Armitage.] Of course, you know, I’m really most anxious about Mabel. How is she?
I think I told you that I was up practically all night with her.
Bodily, no. We supped in the kitchen at two. It’s amazing how emotion stimulates the appetite. No, Clement, her indisposition is of the mind. She wept.
All the time. [Slight pause. Then he adds with a sigh.] I had rather a trying night.

I’m not without experience. Poor dear Mabel’s mother, for instance—one of the best women in the world—she would cry at times, and if she got well off the scratch, she was—er—hard to beat. Mind you, I’ll be fair; I was much to blame—very much to blame. But as for Mabel, bless you, that dear child could have given her poor mother a stone and—er—what’s the expression?
Come, Colonel, give me the message.
I have no message for you. I may tell you, you are not in very great favour. [Gunning smiles.] You’re not well spoken of, Clement.
Oho! Perhaps my wife had a good word for my old friend, Gunning.
In regard to Mr. Gunning, I think the word “serpent” was employed. [Parbury laughs quietly; Gunning becomes serious.] All the same, I have a message for him.
[Rising.] In that case, I’ll get out of the way. I shall be in my study if I’m wanted.
[Comes C.] Very well. But I must say, Clement, that I find you, very much to my surprise and regret, just a little—a little—er—give me a word.
Thanks, yes—callous; and, dearly fond as I am of my daughter, I think I have a right to ask how long you intend leaving your wife on my hands.

lg.l: Shut up, George! [He goes to Armitage.] My dear old friend——

div.p: [Interrupting.] Hear me out, please. My dear daughter is, of course, always more than welcome to my home, but I trust you will not misunderstand me when I say that I require notice. Since I regained my liberty—I mean, since the death of your wife’s dear mother, I’ve drifted into my own—er—little ways. This affair has deranged my plans. Without being indiscreet, I may tell you that I’ve had to send telegrams.

Send her back to me, Colonel. Consult at once your happiness and mine by using your authority. Tell her that cook is in revolt, and that Evans is impertinent. Tell her that I only want my own way when I know I am absolutely right, as in this case. And above all, tell her that I prefer her society to that of a second-class cynic who bellows for champagne at ten o’clock in the morning.
In regard to your son-in-law, Colonel, you have my respectful sympathy.
A good fellow, but inconsiderate. [He lowers his voice.] I may tell you in confidence, Gunning, that I had been looking forward to keeping a rather pleasant appointment to-night——
[He takes a miniature from his pocket and looks at it.
[Leaning towards him.] Might one venture to——
[Keeping the miniature away from him.] Oh, no, no, no, no—wouldn’t be fair. Oh, no. Besides, you might know her hus—you might—er——
Yes, yes, of course; one can’t be too discreet.
[Quickly.] Not, mind you, that there’s anything the whole world mightn’t know, only she—er—she’s not happy at home, and a quiet evening at a theatre—you understand?
Now you, my dear fellow, can do me a friendly turn.
I should be delighted to, but—I don’t see——
I’ll explain. My daughter wishes to see you. She seems to think that you hold the key of the situation.
But I don’t. I should very much object to.
Never mind—never mind! See her and do your utmost to make it up between her and Clement.
To put it bluntly, I shall not be able to keep my appointment to-night if I still have my daughter on my hands.
In which case my friend will be vexed—very vexed. I should have mentioned that on her mother’s side my friend is Spanish.
[Smiling. Shakes hands.] That decides me. Where is your daughter now?

She’s there, my boy, quite close. We walked over the heath together. One moment. [He brings a chair forward.] Would you kindly lend me your arm? [With Gunning’s assistance he mounts a chair, then he raises his hat on his stick.] That’s the signal the coast is clear. Trust an old campaigner. There she is! I say, put that wine away! [Gunning puts the bottle under table up L.C., and places the glasses on table and covers them over with serviette.] It’s all right! Thank you, thank you! [As Gunning helps him down.] Remember, my dear fellow, that I’ve trusted you implicitly. My happiness is in your hands. If we men didn’t stand shoulder to shoulder in these little matters, society would—er—would——

p.hi: Advancing cautiously, she bows very stiffly to

div.p: Well, I’ll leave you. There’s nothing further I can do for you at present, dear?
You might stay in the garden and give me a signal if Clement is coming. I have no intention of meeting him under the circumstances.
Very well, I’ll give you an unmistakable signal. “I’ll sing thee songs of Araby.”
[Grimly.] Well, Mr. Gunning, I hope you’re satisfied with your work.
Oh, I hope you won’t dispute that. Clement and I were living together in perfect harmony, in perfect happiness, until you turned up yesterday.
I was going to say like the snake in the garden.
Better still. Our conversation doesn’t open propitiously. Don’t you think it would conduce to the comfort of us both if we didn’t pursue it any further?
I acknowledge cowardice in regard to other people’s affairs.
Believe me, Mrs. Parbury, you are mistaken. I didn’t interfere in any way.
You aired opinions to me—pernicious opinions. I have a right to assume that you aired the same opinions to Clement, over whom you have some sort of influence.

Not, I think, a good influence, Mr. Gunning. I’ve been thinking things over since midnight. Hitherto I’ve been obliged to think very little of serious things. Perhaps trouble sharpens the intelligence. I’ve discovered that your influence over Clement is the influence of ridicule—the ridicule of the untamed for the tamed.
Say of the disreputable for the respectable, if you like, Mrs. Parbury.
Thank you. That quite expresses my present opinion. Of course it is in your power at least to modify it.
I should be grateful if you would show me the way.
’Pon my word, I am. [Mrs. Parbury raises her hand protestingly.] No, but really—I assure you, dear Mrs. Parbury—I’m not nearly such a bad fellow as you think. What can I do?
Something—anything to remove Miss Woodward from this house.
Miss Woodward! What has she to do with your quarrel with Clement?
Everything. Sit down. [He does so. She makes sure that they are unobserved, then takes a chair next him.] Mr. Gunning, strange as it may appear after all that has occurred, I am going to trust you.
That wretched girl is in love with Clement.
[Starting from his chair as if shot.] What!
Miss Woodward is in love with——
[Laughs—sitting.] No, no, no; I simply can’t believe it.
It seems such a monstrous absurdity.
[Drawing herself up.] I see nothing monstrously absurd in any one falling in love with my husband. I did!
Oh, of course—a charming chap; but she’s such an original girl.
[Indignant.] You infer that I am not?
Not at all, Mrs. Parbury. You are really most interesting.
I don’t think you are very tactful.
You appear to take an interest in Miss Woodward.
[Confused.] Only the interest of the student. I still think you must be mistaken.
[Emphatically.] I caught her in the act of kissing his photograph.
You saw her— [Laughs.] My dear Mrs. Parbury, a day-dream!
A fact. When pressed, she didn’t deny it.
No; I thought it wise not to tell him.
In nine cases out of ten it’s vanity that leads men astray.
[With growing wrath.] Mr. Gunning, we are speaking of my husband.
Yes, yes, dear old Clement has his share of vanity, of course. [Aside.] Damn him!
[Rising indignantly.] How dare you speak like that of my husband! A less vain man doesn’t exist, and what small faults he has concern only him and me—and not you in any way.
I beg ten thousand pardons, Mrs. Parbury. Of course you know Clement far better than I do. Please don’t go.
I shall certainly not remain to hear my husband abused.
No, no; a mistake. Do sit down again.
[Crosses to R.C.] You might, with advantage, look for vanity nearer home, Mr. Gunning.
As for the sort of weakness you were good enough to credit my husband with——
Nothing but a slip of the tongue. Do sit down.
No doubt you have accustomed yourself to judging other men from your own standpoint.
That’s it; quite true! You are always right. Won’t you sit?
[She sits. He sighs with relief, then takes a chair himself.
I’m waiting for a suggestion from you.
That expression seems to me to be unnecessarily harsh, Mrs. Parbury.
Oh, of course, if you defend the girl——
Pardon me, but I have an old-fashioned prejudice against speaking ill of the absent.
I didn’t observe it when you spoke of my husband.
[Laughing.] Fairly hit. Come, let’s be practical. Miss Woodward must not remain in the house, and Clement must not know the truth. On these points we are quite agreed.
Very well. I’ll see Clement. I have an idea.
[Rises.] You’ll not tell him you’ve seen me.
Remember above all, it’s most important to our future happiness that Clement should be the first to give way.
And, Mr. Gunning, if you succeed I’ll try to forget the mischief you’ve created, and will ask you to come and see us—[shakes hands with him]—occasionally.
[Voice of Colonel Armitage outside singing “I’ll sing thee songs of Araby.”
That’s father’s signal. I am going to walk on the heath. I’m far too proud to allow myself to be discovered by Clement here. He might think I want to come back.

[Voice of Armitage, still singing, comes nearer until he enters with Parbury, with the words “or charm thee to a tear.” Unseen by Parbury,
Gunning points out to the Colonel the direction in which Mrs. Parbury has gone.
[In a low voice, to Gunning.] Will it be all right?
[Going R.] Well, I’ll finish my constitutional. I’ll look in again, Clement, in the hope that you will then be able to tell me how long this extremely uncomfortable state of affairs is to last.

[Exit Armitage,
R., singing until he is well off.
[Gunning hands him a cigarette, then takes a cigarette himself. They both smoke. There is a short silence.
Not a stroke of work. It’s absurd!
[Throws cigarette on ground in a rage.
Then how can you expect to do imaginative work?
